candidates.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts.
candidates.author: Mark Twain
candidates.locator: the Conclusion, chapter LXI (American Publishing Company, 1869)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel in the form of a cure: a reader about to spend the day inside one small opinion is told at six in the morning where the antidote is kept.

candidates.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.whyThisMonth: The plainest counsel in the book and the least sentimental: before the mind is asked to do anything, the body has to be fed.

candidates.quote: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
candidates.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
candidates.whyThisMonth: A maxim that becomes advice the moment it is believed: widen the words you have and you widen the day you are able to describe.

candidates.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
candidates.author: William Blake
candidates.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
candidates.whyThisMonth: A proverb Blake wrote himself rather than inherited, and it dignifies an ordinary Tuesday: what gets made inside an hour is what the endless is said to love.

candidates.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
candidates.author: David Hume
candidates.locator: Of the Standard of Taste, paragraph 7 (Miller edition, pp. 229 to 230)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel for anyone about to argue over taste before breakfast: the quarrel is not in the thing, and Hume settles it without scolding anybody.

candidates.quote: The butterfly counts not months but moments, / and has time enough.
candidates.author: Rabindranath Tagore
candidates.locator: the butterfly couplet (Macmillan, 1928); the pieces carry no numbers in that edition
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two lines of counsel about hurry, handed to a reader who has woken up already believing the day is behind.

candidates.quote: When you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
candidates.author: Paulo Coelho
candidates.locator: Part One, the king of Salem to the boy
candidates.speaker: Melchizedek, the king of Salem
candidates.whyThisMonth: The counsel an old king gives a boy who is about to leave, which is this month's shape exactly, and it sends a reader out of the door believing the day is on his side.

candidates.quote: The problem in public life is learning to overcome terror; the problem in married life is learning to overcome boredom.
candidates.author: Gabriel García Márquez
candidates.work: Love in the Time of Cholera
candidates.locator: chapter 4, on Fermina Daza’s married years
candidates.whyThisMonth: A maxim about the two kinds of courage a life asks for, and the second kind is the one an ordinary weekday morning actually needs.

candidates.quote: Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know.
candidates.author: John Keats
candidates.locator: to Fanny Keats, Winchester, 28 August 1819; the manuscript sentence runs on after a dash, so the cut is at a complete clause
candidates.whyThisMonth: A recipe for a well spent day from a man who was given few of them: at six in the morning it reads as counsel about what is actually enough.

candidates.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
candidates.author: Ian Fleming
candidates.locator: Adventure Number Two, the crossing to Calais (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
candidates.speaker: Commander Caractacus Pott
candidates.whyThisMonth: A father's counsel to his children on a morning that has gone sideways, and it answers the exact objection a reader raises at six o'clock.

candidates.quote: It’s a dangerous business, Frodo, going out of your door. You step into the Road, and if you don’t keep your feet, there is no knowing where you might be swept off to.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company; the two halves stand either side of he used to say, so the join needs a note
candidates.speaker: Bilbo Baggins, quoted by Frodo
candidates.whyThisMonth: The counsel a character gives on the way out of the door, which is this month's brief in one sentence, and the book says out of your door where the film says out your door.

candidates.quote: Courage is found in unlikely places.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company
candidates.speaker: Gildor Inglorion
candidates.whyThisMonth: Parting counsel from an elf to a frightened hobbit, five words long, and it survives being read before the day has proved anything.

candidates.author: Albert Camus
candidates.locator: Part One, The Rebel, the closing formula of the chapter
candidates.whyThisMonth: The book's whole argument in four words: what a person refuses tells him who the we is, and the dash is Bower's, not ours.

candidates.quote: Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
candidates.author: Oscar Wilde
candidates.speaker: Gilbert
candidates.whyThisMonth: This is the real text behind the card that travels as Give a man a mask, and as an aphorism about candour it belongs to the month of maxims; Gilbert says it, not Wilde in his own person.
